title: UNIT 4: PERIODIC CLASSIFICATION OF THE ELEMENTS
notes:
✓ The periodic table arranges elements according to their atomic numbers and electron configurations.

→ Elements with similar valence-electron arrangements show similar chemical properties.
→ Periodic trends help predict the behavior of elements across periods and down groups.

title: 4.1 Historical Development of Periodic Classification
notes:
✓ Scientists developed different systems for classifying elements as more elements were discovered.

◆ Major stages:
✓ Döbereiner → Law of Triads.
✓ Newlands → Law of Octaves.
✓ Lothar Meyer → periodic relationship between atomic volume and atomic mass.
✓ Mendeleev → periodic table based mainly on atomic mass and chemical properties.
✓ Modern periodic table → arranged according to atomic number.

title: 4.1.1 Law of Triads
notes:
✓ Döbereiner grouped some elements into sets of three called triads.

◆ In a triad:
✓ Elements had similar chemical properties.
✓ The atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the average of the other two.

◆ Example:
Li, Na, K.

→ The system was useful but could classify only a limited number of elements.

title: 4.1.2 Law of Octaves
notes:
✓ Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing atomic mass and observed that every eighth element had similar properties, similar to the repetition of musical notes.

✓ Limitation → the pattern worked mainly for lighter elements and became unreliable for heavier elements.

title: 4.1.3 Lothar Meyer's Curve
notes:
✓ Lothar Meyer showed periodicity by plotting atomic volume against atomic mass.

→ The graph showed repeating patterns in the physical properties of elements, supporting the idea that properties vary periodically with atomic mass.

→ His work contributed to the development of the periodic classification.

title: 4.2 Mendeleev's Classification
notes:
✓ Mendeleev arranged elements mainly in order of increasing atomic mass and placed elements with similar chemical properties in the same groups.

◆ Major achievements:
✓ Left gaps for undiscovered elements.
✓ Predicted properties of some undiscovered elements.
✓ Corrected the position of some elements when chemical properties disagreed with atomic mass order.

✓ Limitation → atomic mass could not correctly explain the position of some elements and isotopes.

title: 4.2.1 Periodic Law
notes:
✓ Modern periodic law states:

"The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers."

→ When elements are arranged by increasing atomic number, similar properties recur at regular intervals.

title: 4.3 Modern Periodic Table
notes:
✓ The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number.

◆ It contains:
✓ 7 periods → horizontal rows.
✓ 18 groups → vertical columns.

→ Elements in the same group generally have similar chemical properties because they have similar valence-electron configurations.

title: 4.3.1 Period
notes:
✓ Period → a horizontal row in the periodic table.

✓ There are 7 periods.

→ The period number corresponds to the highest principal energy level occupied by electrons in the ground-state atom.

→ Across a period, atomic number increases by one from one element to the next.

title: 4.3.2 Group
notes:
✓ Group → a vertical column in the periodic table.

✓ There are 18 groups.

→ Elements in the same group generally have similar valence-electron configurations and therefore similar chemical properties.

◆ Examples:
✓ Group 1 → alkali metals.
✓ Group 17 → halogens.
✓ Group 18 → noble gases.

title: 4.3.3 Electron Configuration and Periodicity
notes:
✓ The periodicity of elements is closely related to their electron configurations.

✓ Period number → highest occupied principal energy level.
✓ Group similarity → similar valence-electron configuration.
✓ Valence electrons → strongly influence chemical properties.

→ As atomic number increases, electrons are added according to the rules of electron configuration, producing repeating chemical behavior.

title: 4.4 Atomic Size
notes:
✓ Atomic size → describes the relative size of an atom and is commonly represented by atomic radius.

◆ Trend:
✓ Across a period → generally decreases.
✓ Down a group → generally increases.

◆ Reason:
→ Across a period, effective nuclear attraction increases.
→ Down a group, additional electron shells increase the size of the atom.

title: 4.4.1 Ionization Energy
notes:
✓ Ionization energy → the minimum energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

◆ Trend:
✓ Across a period → generally increases.
✓ Down a group → generally decreases.

→ Attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons becomes stronger across a period and weaker down a group.

title: 4.4.2 Electron Affinity
notes:
✓ Electron affinity → describes the energy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom to form a negative ion.

→ In general, atoms toward the right side of a period tend to have a greater tendency to gain electrons, especially halogens.

✓ The trend is less uniform than atomic size or ionization energy because electron-electron repulsions and subshell structure affect the values.

title: 4.4.3 Electronegativity
notes:
✓ Electronegativity → the ability of an atom in a chemical bond to attract the shared electrons toward itself.

◆ Trend:
✓ Across a period → generally increases.
✓ Down a group → generally decreases.

✓ Fluorine has the highest electronegativity.

title: 4.4.4 Major Periodic Trends
notes:
◆ Across a period:
✓ Atomic size ↓
✓ Ionization energy ↑
✓ Electronegativity ↑
✓ Metallic character ↓

◆ Down a group:
✓ Atomic size ↑
✓ Ionization energy ↓
✓ Electronegativity ↓
✓ Metallic character ↑

◆ REMEMBER
✓ Atomic size → increases down and to the left.
✓ Ionization energy → increases up and to the right.
✓ Electronegativity → increases up and to the right.

title: UNIT 4 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ Döbereiner → Law of Triads.
✓ Newlands → Law of Octaves.
✓ Lothar Meyer → atomic volume curve.
✓ Mendeleev → periodic table based mainly on atomic mass and properties.
✓ Modern table → atomic number.

✓ Modern periodic law → properties are periodic functions of atomic number.

✓ Period → horizontal row.
✓ Group → vertical column.

◆ Atomic size:
✓ Across → decreases.
✓ Down → increases.

◆ Ionization energy:
✓ Across → increases.
✓ Down → decreases.

◆ Electronegativity:
✓ Across → increases.
✓ Down → decreases.

✓ Electron affinity → energy change associated with adding an electron to a gaseous atom; trends are less regular.

✓ Electron configuration → explains periodicity.
✓ Valence electrons → strongly determine chemical properties.

◆ EXAM TIP
Think of the periodic table as a map of electron configuration. Similar valence-electron arrangements produce similar chemical behavior.
